title: The user interview
summary: Write five questions that open people up, interview the person your build is for, listen harder than you talk, and report what the interview changed in your plan.
materials: notebook and pencil for interview notes
the person your build is for, or a call with them, for ten minutes

steps.title: This week you mostly do not talk
steps.body:
Every Speak week so far, the job was to say things well. This week flips it: the job is to hear things well. You are building something for a real person, and the most expensive mistake a builder can make is to build a beautiful answer to the wrong question. Real engineers guard against it the same way you will: they go and interview the user.

Two kinds of questions exist. Closed questions snap shut in one word: do you like reading in bed? Yes. Open questions swing wide and let the person wander: tell me about the last time something around the house really annoyed you. The wandering is the treasure. People reveal what they actually want in the middle of a story, almost never in a yes or a no.

The interviewer's three habits, and they are all listening habits. One, after you ask, wait. Count three silent seconds after they seem done, because the best sentence often comes limping out last. Two, say it back: so what I heard is, and then their point in your words. If they say no, not quite, you just caught a misunderstanding while it was still cheap to fix. Three, do not defend. If they say something that pokes a hole in your lovely plan, the answer is tell me more, never actually, you see, my design already handles that.

One special rule for gift builders: if your build is still a surprise, interview around the problem, not the present. You can ask someone what makes their mornings annoying without ever saying I am building you a thing for your mornings.

The question of the week sits under all of it: can you ever really know what someone else wants? Hold onto it during the interview, because you are about to feel exactly how hard knowing another person is. Watch what happens when an answer surprises you. A surprise means the picture of that person you were carrying around had a wrong bit in it, and you only found the wrong bit because you asked and then stopped talking. It cuts both ways, and you will probably feel both sides in the same ten minutes: asking got you closer than guessing ever could, and asking also showed you how much of them you had been making up.

So the week ends in the ring. Tonight's motion is 'You can never really know what someone else wants', three rounds, either side, and you steelman the other side before you answer it. Your notebook is the evidence whichever side you take: the answers you could have written down yourself beforehand, and the two you circled because you could not. Your recording still ends on your own answer.

steps.title: Write five questions that open
steps.body:
Write five interview questions for your person in your notebook, and make them earn their place.

The shape to aim for: at least three of the five start with what, how, or tell me about. None of the five can be finished with just a yes or a no. And the set should cover three jobs: at least one question about the problem itself and when it bites, at least one about what annoys them most about how things are now, and at least one about what better would look like in their own words, which you get by asking something like: if this problem vanished tomorrow, what would you do differently?

Two traps to check for before you call the list done. The leading question, which smuggles the answer you want inside it: do you not think a stand would be great? That is fishing for a compliment, not interviewing. And the robot march: five questions read off a list in a row, no matter what the person said. Your list is a map, not a script. If their answer to question one opens a door, walk through it and come back to the list after.

Practice once, out loud, alone: ask your five questions to the empty room and listen to how they sound. Fix any that sound like a quiz.
checklist: Five questions are written, and at least three start with what, how, or tell me about
None of the five can be answered with only a yes or a no
The set covers the problem, the biggest annoyance, and what better would look like
No question smuggles in the answer I am hoping for

steps.title: The interview
steps.body:
Ten minutes with your person, notebook open, plan out of sight. Tell them the honest truth about what this is: I am making something and I want to understand the problem better, so I have five questions and mostly I want to listen.

Run your habits. Ask, then wait the three seconds. Jot short notes while they talk, just enough words to find the thought again, and finish the note after they stop rather than making them watch you write. At least twice in the interview, say a point back in your own words, so what I heard is, and let them correct you. Corrections are the interview working, not failing.

When an answer surprises you, that is the signal to dig once more: tell me more about that. The surprising answers are worth double, because they are the ones your plan did not already contain.

End by thanking them, and then, only after the interview is truly over, look at your notes next to your plan. Circle the two most surprising things they said. Then write one sentence at the bottom of the page: what this interview changes in my plan, or, if it truly changes nothing, what it confirmed and why you believe the interview really tested the plan rather than just petting it.
checklist: I asked all five questions and waited out the quiet after each one
I said their point back in my own words at least twice
I did not defend my plan or pitch my build, even once
The two most surprising answers are circled in my notes
One sentence at the bottom says what changes in the plan, or what was confirmed and how the interview really tested it

steps.title: Record the report
steps.prompt: Record your interview report in under three minutes: the five questions you asked, the two most surprising answers said back in the person's own words as closely as you can, and the one thing that now changes in your plan, or the thing the interview confirmed. Close the recording with your answer to the question of the week: can you ever really know what someone else wants?
